section_1.title: The Cheetah's Sprint: A Real-World Mystery
section_1.content: Introduce the relationship between speed and distance using a character. Establish the core question: If we know a cheetah's instantaneous speed at every second, how can we calculate the total distance it ran?
section_1.example: An animated cheetah named 'Dash' sprints across the screen. A graph above him shows his velocity curve. As Dash speeds up, the line on the graph climbs. We want to find the total distance covered.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Review: The Derivative as a Slope
section_2.content: Briefly recap the derivative to ensure a solid foundation. Define it visually as the 'slope of the tangent line' or the 'rate of change.'
section_2.example: Show a car climbing a hill. The derivative is represented by a glowing 'inclinometer' showing the steepness (slope) at every specific point on the hill's curve.

section_3.title: The Integral: Accumulation of Tiny Slices
section_3.content: Introduce the integral not as a formula, but as a geometric concept: the area under a curve. Explain that this area represents the 'accumulation' of a quantity over time.
section_3.example: In Dash the Cheetah’s velocity graph, the area under the line is sliced into thousands of thin vertical rectangles. As these rectangles fill with color, they represent the total distance being 'collected' or accumulated.

section_4.title: The Bridge: The Inverse Operation
section_4.content: Explain the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: Integration and Differentiation are opposites. If differentiation 'breaks' a function down into its rate of change, integration 'builds' it back up into its total accumulation.
section_4.example: Visualizing a 'Math Machine': Put a 'Position' function in, the 'Derivative Gear' turns it into 'Velocity.' Put that 'Velocity' into the 'Integral Gear' (turning in the opposite direction), and it spits back the original 'Position' function.

section_5.title: The Geometric Proof: Why the Rate of Area is the Height
section_5.content: Use a dynamic visual to show that the rate at which the 'Area under the curve' grows is exactly equal to the height of the curve at that point. This is the 'A-ha!' moment linking the two concepts.
section_5.example: An animation shows a shaded area under a curve $f(x)$ moving to the right. A small sliver of width 'dx' is added. The height of this sliver is $f(x)$. Therefore, the change in area ($dA$) divided by the change in width ($dx$) is the height $f(x)$.

section_6.title: Summary: Two Sides of the Same Coin
section_6.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that the derivative tells you how fast you're changing, while the integral tells you how much you've changed in total.
section_6.example: Split screen: On the left, a character climbing stairs (derivative = step height). On the right, the character filling a bucket with water (integral = total volume). The screen merges to show the final formula: $\int a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)$.

outline.title: The Bridge: The Inverse Operation
outline.content: Explain the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: Integration and Differentiation are opposites. If differentiation 'breaks' a function down into its rate of change, integration 'builds' it back up into its total accumulation.
outline.example: Visualizing a 'Math Machine': Put a 'Position' function in, the 'Derivative Gear' turns it into 'Velocity.' Put that 'Velocity' into the 'Integral Gear' (turning in the opposite direction), and it spits back the original 'Position' function.

storyboard.title: The Bridge: The Inverse Operation
lecture_lines: Differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus links them.
Differentiation breaks a function down into its rate.
Integration builds that rate back into the whole.
They are two directions on the same mathematical road.
animations: Display a 'Position' box s(t) on the left side (#FFFFFF).
Show a 'Derivative Gear' turning s(t) into 'Velocity' v(t) (#00FF00).
Display a 'Velocity' box v(t) in the middle (#00FFFF).
Show an 'Integral Gear' turning v(t) back into s(t) (#FF00FF).
Flash both gears to emphasize they are inverse operations (#FFFF00).

outline.title: The Geometric Proof: Why the Rate of Area is the Height
outline.content: Use a dynamic visual to show that the rate at which the 'Area under the curve' grows is exactly equal to the height of the curve at that point. This is the 'A-ha!' moment linking the two concepts.
outline.example: An animation shows a shaded area under a curve $f(x)$ moving to the right. A small sliver of width 'dx' is added. The height of this sliver is $f(x)$. Therefore, the change in area ($dA$) divided by the change in width ($dx$) is the height $f(x)$.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Proof: Why the Rate of Area is the Height
lecture_lines: Watch the area grow as we move right.
A tiny sliver adds a bit more area.
The height of this sliver is the function's value.
The rate of area growth equals the curve's height.
This proves that the derivative of area is height.
animations: Show a function f(x) with a shaded area A(x) below it (#00FFFF).
Animate the shaded area growing by a small width dx (#FFFFFF).
Highlight the added sliver with height f(x) in green (#00FF00).
Show the formula dA = f(x) * dx appearing near the sliver (#FF8C00).
Transform the formula into dA/dx = f(x) with emphasis (#FF00FF).

outline.title: The Cheetah's Sprint: A Real-World Mystery
outline.content: Introduce the relationship between speed and distance using a character. Establish the core question: If we know a cheetah's instantaneous speed at every second, how can we calculate the total distance it ran?
outline.example: An animated cheetah named 'Dash' sprints across the screen. A graph above him shows his velocity curve. As Dash speeds up, the line on the graph climbs. We want to find the total distance covered.

storyboard.title: The Cheetah's Sprint: A Real-World Mystery
lecture_lines: Meet Dash, a cheetah in full sprint.
We know his exact speed at every moment.
But how far did Dash actually travel?
animations: Display an animated cheetah 'Dash' sprinting at the bottom (#FFFF00).
Show a velocity curve v(t) appearing above the cheetah (#00FFFF).
Highlight the area under the curve with a pulse effect (#FF00FF).

outline.title: The Integral: Accumulation of Tiny Slices
outline.content: Introduce the integral not as a formula, but as a geometric concept: the area under a curve. Explain that this area represents the 'accumulation' of a quantity over time.
outline.example: In Dash the Cheetah’s velocity graph, the area under the line is sliced into thousands of thin vertical rectangles. As these rectangles fill with color, they represent the total distance being 'collected' or accumulated.

storyboard.title: The Integral: Accumulation of Tiny Slices
lecture_lines: Meet the integral, the tool for accumulation.
It calculates the total area under a curve.
Imagine slicing this area into infinitely thin rectangles.
Adding these slices together gives us the total distance.
Integration turns rates back into total amounts.
animations: Show the velocity graph from the first section (#00FFFF).
Fill the area under the curve with thin vertical rectangles (#FF00FF).
Scale up the sum of rectangles to show total distance (#FFFF00).

outline.title: Prerequisite Review: The Derivative as a Slope
outline.content: Briefly recap the derivative to ensure a solid foundation. Define it visually as the 'slope of the tangent line' or the 'rate of change.'
outline.example: Show a car climbing a hill. The derivative is represented by a glowing 'inclinometer' showing the steepness (slope) at every specific point on the hill's curve.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Review: The Derivative as a Slope
lecture_lines: Recall the derivative measures the rate of change.
Visually, it is the slope of the tangent line.
It tells us how steep a curve is here.
animations: Show a car climbing a curved hill path (#FFFFFF).
Draw a glowing tangent line at a specific point (#00FF00).
Label the slope of the tangent line as f'(x) (#FF8C00).
